processing: A tea plant variety, not a finished tea; it is used for green tea, which means quick fixing and drying with no oxidation.
appearance_dry: As green tea, typical of Xinyang teas: dark green, fine leaf, though little is documented for this variety alone.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green, as is typical of Xinyang green teas.
appearance_wet: Plump shoots with a moderate coat of down.
taste_profile: Green tea from it is described as distinctly aromatic and full in the mouth; no more detailed tasting record is available.

brewing.notes: General green tea handling, since the variety is rarely sold under its own name.

vintage_note: Not normally sold under its own name. Leaf from this variety goes into Xinyang-area green teas, which are sold as the current year's spring harvest, as is usual for the class.
description:
Cheyun Zhong is a local tea plant rather than a tea you will find on a shelf: a variety centred on Cheyun Mountain in Xinyang, Henan, the area behind some of the best-known Xinyang green tea.

It is a low shrub with a half-spreading habit and medium-sized, long oval leaves that are bright green and smooth. It reproduces by seed rather than by cutting, which makes it a diploid sexual variety, and plants from seed vary, so growers are advised to select seedlings before planting out. It is a mid-season plant.

The shoots are plump with moderate down, and 100 one-bud-three-leaf shoots weigh about 57 g. Yield is middling and the shoots grow vigorously. Green tea made from it is described as aromatic and full, which fits the general picture of Xinyang greens, though little is recorded about the cup of this variety alone.

If you want to taste this terroir, look for a Cheyun Mountain maojian from a seller who can talk about the garden. Few sellers will name the plant variety, so treat any such claim as something to ask about.
history: Little is documented about the origin of this variety. It is recorded as the local plant of the Cheyun Mountain area, without a named breeder or a date, which fits a seed-grown population rather than a bred cultivar.
